title: The hidden dark side of NGC 24
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 24, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 24 · constellation Sculptor · about 25 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Blue bursts of young stars, dark lanes of dust and red bubbles of hydrogen gas pepper the spiral arms of NGC 24, with distant galaxies hovering around its edge. The galaxy lies about 25 million light-years away in Sculptor and measures some 40 000 light-years across, seen here by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Astronomers suspect that spirals like NGC 24 and the Milky Way sit inside extended haloes of dark matter, a mysterious substance that cannot be seen and reveals itself only through its gravitational pull on surrounding material. About 80% of NGC 24's mass is thought to lie in such a halo.

Dark matter was originally suggested because the outer regions of galaxies, including ours, spin surprisingly quickly. It is also thought to play an essential part in how galaxies form and evolve. The galaxy itself was discovered by the British astronomer William Herschel in 1785.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.86 x 2.94 arcminutes) and distance (25 million light years), the frame spans roughly 21,000 × 21,000 light-years. Its light set out about 25 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The caption links blue to young stars and red to hydrogen gas, but the per-filter mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Dark matter can't be seen at all, and the near-infrared light here is also invisible to the eye.
